voluminous

vuh-LOO-muh-nuhs -- from Latin volumen, 'a roll or scroll,' from volvere, 'to roll.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Voluminous is large in volume or space.

The professor's voluminous lecture notes filled three overflowing binders by the end of the semester.

Example

A wedding gown designer adds layer after layer of tulle until the skirt is voluminous enough to fill an entire doorway.

Voluminous describes exactly that sheer bulk and size -- whether of fabric, hair, writing, or anything else.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

capacious: Capacious is about what something can hold: a capacious suitcase or hall swallows a great deal. Voluminous is about the size of the thing itself -- a voluminous cloak or report is enormous in its own bulk, whether or not it holds anything at all.

expansive: Expansive describes something spread out wide -- an expansive lawn or an expansive view reaching to the horizon. Voluminous is about bulk and fullness rather than spread: fabric, hair, or paperwork swelling in volume instead of stretching across space.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

compact: small and neatly arranged

skimpy: scant or barely enough

Where it sits · how burdensome the size becomes

ample → voluminous → bulky

ample vs. voluminous: Ample is milder than voluminous -- an ample supply or an ample room is comfortably more than enough, while voluminous describes a size so striking that people stop and remark on it.

bulky vs. voluminous: Bulky is stronger and clumsier than voluminous -- bulky suggests something large enough to be awkward or hard to carry, while voluminous simply means large in volume, which can still look graceful, like flowing robes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — volumin-: a roll, scroll (from Latin volumen, voluminis, 'a roll' -- itself from volvere, 'to roll')

Suffix — -ous: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together: Voluminous comes from Latin volumen, voluminis, 'a roll or scroll' -- itself from volvere, 'to roll': volumin- + -ous ('full of'). A large amount of writing had to be rolled into a bulky scroll, so voluminous came to describe anything large in volume or space.

Use the root in a new word: revolve: The observation deck slowly revolves, giving visitors a full view of the city skyline every twenty minutes.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Voluminous most often describes physical size -- clothing, hair, or containers -- but it's also commonly used for writing or paperwork that has grown unusually large, as in 'voluminous notes' or 'a voluminous report.'
